Pelindaba

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After working on apartheid SA's secret atomic weapons programme, hundreds of workers who were injured at Pelindaba are pinning their last hope of getting compensated on the Public Protector.

Summary:
Decades after being employed by the apartheid government at Pelindaba, hundreds of workers have been struggling together for the last 16 years to get compensation for debilitating illnesses that were probably caused by exposure to radiation or harmful chemicals.
Over the years, workers at Pelindaba's test plants had been exposed to chemically toxic and radio-active materials that would react with their skin and organs and now, 20 or 30 years later, cause them to become very ill.
No process for assessing occupational injury and disease was put in place -- the workers had nowhere to go in the company, or in the rest of government, to get their medical records, get independent medical advice and ensure fair compensation for job-related injury.
In most cases, workers who were injured on the job, were summarily retrenched or let go without due process.
It is not known how many workers died on the job, but we have stories of workers who died due to chemical exposure, even before they reached hospitals, and their families were none the wiser.
We also have stories of workers' families now coming to the fore with questions about whether their parents' ill health now could have been caused at Pelindaba all those years ago.
Under pressure to build Apartheid's nuclear bombs, a culture of cutting corners and working without proper oversight and protective gear took root.
Now the chickens are coming home to roost, but in the context of Eskom and the government's stated commitment to nuclear power expansion, the workers have been ignored, intimidated, sent from pillar to post and dumped.
Their last hope is that Public Protector Thuli Madonsela will take them seriously before she leaves office in October.

Press Release:


Pelindaba - Nuclear Wake
Employed by apartheid South Africa’s secret atomic weapons program, hundreds of former Pelindaba workers claim they were unknowingly exposed to toxic and radioactive chemicals. Those still alive suffer from debilitating illnesses and have turned to the Public Protector in hopes of finally getting compensation.



Script:


PELINDABA
In the hills West of Pretoria lies Pelindaba – the home of the South African government’s nuclear research facility.
BONGANI LINK: It looks fairly innocuous now but this was once one of South Africa’s most strategic resources. This is the site where our nuclear weapons were developed – needless to say everything that went on here was top-secret.
Built in the 1960s with help from the United States’ Atoms for Peace program, Pelindaba was said to be for research but at the height of the Cold War, the enriched uranium produced here would no doubt have given the US an advantage.
By the early 1990s former President FW de Klerk admitted that seven nuclear bombs HAD been built – a show of force against the so-called Swart Gevaar advancing through neighbouring countries.
But there remains shroud of uncertainty remains drawn around the devices and the people who worked there.
White men injured in what was then regular accidents on site have had an uphill battle for compensation.
For the many black workers who say they were hurt in the mad rush to destroy all traces of the weapons program before the dawn of a new South Africa, it has proven nearly impossible.
In neighbouring Atteridgeville, Alfred Sepepe watches as one former colleague after another dies. A cleaner at Pelindaba from 1991, he says he sometimes wiped up unknown chemicals without protective clothing – as result he had an operation to have his testicles removed.
ALFRED SEPEPE, FORMER PELINDABA CLEANER: It was the time of Apartheid. When you asked the supervisor, he’d say, “If you don’t want to work, you can go. There are many people looking for work.”
The Public Protector is the last hope for the former workers led by Sepepe. They’ve been fighting since 2000 for compensation from Necsa, now the state company in charge of Pelindaba, for the harm they believe was done to them.
German environmental activist Dr Stefan Cramer, who headed the foundation that first funded research into Pelindaba’s workers, says exposure to radioactive materials can easily happen.
DR STEFAN CRAMER, SCIENCE ADVISER, SA FAITH COMMUNITIES’ ENVIRONMENT INITIATIVE: During accidental releases, usually radioactive dust and radioactive particles are released into the atmosphere and you can be sitting in your garden outside of Pelindaba and out of the blue a little radioactive particle settles in your lung and creates lung cancer.
Dr David Fig was a member of Earthlife Africa, which undertook the research.
DR DAVID FIG, INDEPENDENT ENERGY RESEARCHER: There was a lot of downsizing at Necsa. From the early 90s there were attempts to dismantle the weapons program which actually meant decontaminating a lot of buildings. A lot of workers may have been used in that process without the prior informed consent about how much exposure they would have to radioactive materials.
ALFRED SEPEPE, FORMER PELINDABA CLEANER: When it was teatime, we would go out of the area, I opened the door, took off my dustcoat and put my hands and feet into the machine – the machine would light up red – that means my hands were not clean and I would wash my hands – I went back to wash my hands and it would still be red.
BONGANI: So when did you get sick?
ALFRED SEPEPE: In 1996 I couldn’t work anymore. When I went to urinate, I felt so much pain I used to scream “aow” – blood started to come out before the urine.
Earthlife Africa appointed an occupational health specialist to assess complaints and examine workers. Activist Mashile Phalane realised what all researchers have seen – without full employment and medical files, it’s nearly impossible to prove how the workers got sick.
MASHILE PHALANE, FORMER EARTHLIFE AFRICA ACTIVIST: Each one signed a medical request to Necsa to say I need my medical records.
Earthlife’s report lamented major gaps in the workers’ records from Necsa.
Amanda Daniels joined the workers from Atteridgeville in their search for answers. Widowed at the age of 45 when her husband died from cancer, she learned only later that he believed it was from radiation released when he helped to fight a fire.
AMANDA DANIELS, WIDOW OF PELINDABA SECURITY GUARD: He always told the children they’re not allowed to touch his shoes, when we had to clean his shoes. They were not allowed to talk about what went on there. They could never say anything about Pelindaba.
Daniels was one of a group that Mashile Phalane and David Fig took to Parliament to speak truth to power.
AMANDA DANIELS (in Parliament): I feel that Necsa owes me an explanation – compensation for the terrible loss.
MASHILE PHALANE: It was the first time they approached the Parliament – the lobbyists from nuclear industry is very strong so that thing end there.
Johan Janse van Rensburg’s case shows what a person fighting against Necsa alone, can be up against. In 1982 he was doing repairs when a pipe containing uranium hexafluoride exploded in his face.
JOHAN JANSE VAN RENSBURG, FORMER PELINDABA PROCESS OPERATOR: It’s like a dense smoke around me and I inhaled a lot of it. Then my foreman at the time, he had never issued a work permit for me in which he specified which protective gear I should use. So they quickly wrote out the work permit and with my eyes closed from the burning, I can still remember how they took my hand and put it in the spot where I had to sign and then I just signed.
After retrenchment in 1995, Janse van Rensburg realised his troubles had just begun. Expert physician Prof. James Ker examined Van Rensburg and says only exposure to uranium hexafluoride can explain why the former avid sportsman now faces old age constantly short of breath, with half his lung capacity.
PROF. JAMES KER, SPECIALIST PHYSICIAN: After the event, at 02:45 in the morning, this concentration in his urine of uranium, shot up to a documented 3519 micrograms per litre. It elevated by almost 2000. Then it dropped. So we have documented proof that this man was exposed to a significant amount of uranium. 24 years later, I saw him with respiratory symptoms. He had multiple areas of fibrosis, which is scar tissue in his lungs – this did not follow any pattern of any known documented lung disease known to the medical industry.
Attorney Gert van der Merwe says Necsa resisted claims for compensation, pointing to a cheque from the Compensation Fund in 1982 – for R215,35.
GERT VAN DER MERWE, VAN RENSBURG’S ATTORNEY: They raised a plea of preclusion in terms of the 1941 Compensation Act…when an employee filed a claim against the compensation commissioner, he is precluded from filing a lawsuit against his employer. I think it’s unconstitutional to preclude him from, now when he realises his injuries, instituting action against that entity.
The Workmen’s Compensation Fund said it dealt with 1918 claims from Necsa employees between 1980 and 2014 for, among others, lung conditions such as asthma and asbestosis, and skin conditions like dermatitis.
BONGANI LINK: Necsa initially agreed to our request for an on-camera interview but when we sent them our list of questions, saying they would rather wait for the Public Protector’s report on the matter.
The National Nuclear Regulator, or NNR, also wouldn’t speak to us. Investigator Elsabe de Waal accompanied Advocate Thuli Madonsela to Atteridgeville to interview about 300 former workers.
ADV. ELSABE DE WAAL, CHIEF INVESTIGATOR, PUBLIC PROTECTOR: In 2010, when we were approached by Earthlife Africa, at that stage, our office was so inundated with complaints. So our office took a decision to outsource this investigation. By 2014 we saw that there was no real progress and the Public Protector took the decision to bring the matter back to us. And then we really had to restart the investigation from scratch. We have already drafted a provisional report which we have submitted to the Public Protector for her inputs.
The final report is expected in a few months’ time. First, seven of the workers have been asked to undergo renewed medical tests locally with oversight by a United Nations specialist.
ADV. ELSABE DE WAAL: It will be a very expensive exercise but the NNR said that they’d be willing to do that.
The fact that the Nuclear Regulator is paying for the tests, fuels the workers’ and activists’ concerns about independence of the process.
DR STEFAN CRAMER: Basically all excellent South African nuclear scientists have been involved in government programs at one stage or another or are dependent on government contracts.
There have been drastic changes at Necsa in the last decade to make it safer for workers, but in light of government’s plans for new nuclear power stations, not everyone is convinced.
DR DAVID FIG: By squeezing out the possibility of workers making compensation claims, they prove that it’s a safe industry ’cause there are no statistics that show the damage that is being done. I think it’s absolutely essential that we hold the industry to account in improving all this before expansion goes ahead.
